planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or bog gardens in consistently moist to saturated, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, with the crown sitting at or just above the waterline; this fully double form is sterile and produces no seed, so it is propagated only by division of the rhizomatous clump.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or bog gardens in consistently moist to saturated, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade, with the crown at or just above the waterline. Flore Pleno is a long-cultivated sport of native marsh marigold bearing fully double, tightly packed, pompom-like golden-yellow flowers in place of the species' simple buttercup blooms, opening in early to mid spring above clumps of glossy, rounded, deep-green leaves. Because the flowers are sterile and set no seed, the plant channels its energy into a long, showy bloom period and spreads slowly by rhizome rather than self-sowing, making it a well-behaved choice for formal pond margins and bog garden borders. Divide congested clumps every 3-4 years in fall or early spring to maintain vigor and flower quality.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or bog gardens in consistently moist to saturated, humus-rich soil in full sun; this compact Himalayan variety flowers slightly earlier and stays noticeably smaller than the common yellow-flowered species.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring at the margins of ponds, streams, or bog gardens in consistently moist to saturated, humus-rich soil in full sun. Caltha palustris var. alba is a naturally occurring white-flowered form of marsh marigold from the Himalayan foothills, forming a compact clump of glossy, kidney-shaped leaves topped by creamy-white, buttercup-like flowers with a bright yellow-stamened center, opening a little earlier in spring than the typical yellow-flowered species. It is smaller and slightly less floriferous than common marsh marigold but often produces a light second flush of bloom later in the season, and its pale flowers offer a useful color contrast at the pond edge among yellow flag iris and blue-flowered aquatics. Give it the same wet-margin conditions as C. palustris and divide every few years to maintain a tight, floriferous clump.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in shallow water up to 6 inches deep or saturated soil at pond or stream margins in full sun to partial shade once soil has warmed in spring; grow in a submerged container to contain its spreading rhizomes in smaller water gardens.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in shallow water up to 6 inches deep or consistently saturated soil at pond or stream margins in full sun to partial shade; Asian lizard's tail is the East Asian counterpart to the native American Saururus cernuus, native to wetlands, ditches, and marshes across China, Japan, Korea, and the Philippines. It forms upright clumps of heart-shaped, prominently veined green leaves and produces arching, drooping spikes of small fragrant white flowers through summer, giving the plant its common name. Slightly more sun-loving and a bit taller-growing than the American species, it spreads steadily by rhizome to form dense colonies at the water's edge and works well as a bold textural companion to pickerelweed and native iris in a water garden. Divide every few years in spring to control spread and reinvigorate the clump.

planting.note: Divide established clumps and plant rhizomes in spring in acidic, sandy or peaty aquatic soil in containers placed at the pond margin in full sun to partial shade, in water up to 6 inches deep; keep the crown consistently wet and never let it dry out.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in acidic, sandy or peaty aquatic soil at pond margins in water up to 6 inches deep in full sun to partial shade; spoonflower is a smaller, more delicate southeastern relative of the more widespread arrow arum, native to acidic blackwater swamps and pocosin wetlands of the Coastal Plain from Virginia to Louisiana. Its narrower, spoon-shaped arrowhead leaves are more compact than those of Peltandra virginica, and it bears a distinctive white-hooded spathe wrapped around a yellow spadix from spring into late summer, a much longer and showier bloom season than its common cousin. It forms slow-spreading, well-behaved colonies rather than aggressive stands, making it a good choice for smaller acidic bog gardens and rain gardens as well as pond edges. All parts contain calcium oxalate and are irritating if chewed or eaten.
